title: Quench, Glow, or Stay Silent: Distance-Controlled Up-Conversion Emission near Metallic Nanowires
authors: Maciej Cwierzona, Michal Zebrowski, Pavel Dziarhai, Joanna Niedziolka-Jonsson, Martin Jonsson-Niedziolka, Marcin Nyk, Sebastian Mackowski, Dawid Piatkowski
abstract: We demonstrate controlled transitions between competing radiative and nonradiative decay channels in the up-conversion luminescence of NaYF4:Er3+/Yb3+ nanocrystals placed in proximity to metallic nanowires. The nanocrystal-nanowire separation is used as a key control parameter governing the optical response. An essential aspect of our approach is the removal of inhomogeneous residual polymer layers from the nanowires, eliminating any compromise on distance control and reproducibility in emitter-metal hybrid nanostructures. Replacing them with a well-defined polymer spacer yields controlled access to three qualitatively distinct interaction regimes: luminescence quenching, plasmonic enhancement, and effective decoupling. Transitions between these regimes are shown to reflect changes in the dominant energy relaxation pathways: from nonradiative losses in direct contact with the metal, through modification of the local photonic density of states and coupling to plasmon-mediated modes, to behavior characteristic of quasi-isolated emitters. The plasmonic origin of the emission enhancement in the intermediate regime is evidenced by an increase in luminescence intensity accompanied by shortened decay times, as revealed by fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy of up-conversion nanocrystals. All experiments were performed on single nanostructures, thereby excluding artefacts arising from aggregation effects and strengthening the interpretation of the observed phenomena. The presented approach provides controlled access to plasmon-modified decay channels and offers a basis for the rational design of functional nanophotonic and sensing structures with tailored optical properties.
summary: The authors developed a highly controlled hybrid nanostructure combining rare-earth up-conversion nanocrystals with metallic nanowires separated by a polymer spacer. By tuning this separation distance, they demonstrated deterministic control over the optical response, observing transitions between luminescence quenching, plasmon-enhanced emission, and near-decoupled behavior.
main_problem: The research aims to achieve precise, reproducible control over the interaction between individual up-conversion emitters and metallic nanostructures to study distance-dependent emission modification.
main_result: Three distinct optical regimes—quenching, plasmonic enhancement, and effective decoupling—were demonstrated by systematically controlling the separation distance using a polymer spacer layer.
method: The study utilized single-nanostructure measurements with time-resolved microsecond fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) under 980 nm excitation.
model_or_system: The platform consists of $	ext{NaYF}_4:	ext{Er}^{3+}/	ext{Yb}^{3+}$ nanocrystals placed near silver nanowires, separated by a precisely controlled polymer spacer film like PVA. This hybrid architecture allows tuning the emitter-metal coupling.
key_observables: Emission intensity maps (PL), fluorescence decay times ($\mu	ext{s-FLIM}$), and the separation distance ($d$).
important_parameters: Separation distance ($d$), which controls transitions between quenching, enhancement, and decoupling regimes.
main_assumptions: The use of a well-defined polymer spacer overcomes limitations from inhomogeneous residual layers found in previous studies. The observed enhancement is attributed to modification of the local photonic density of states coupled to plasmon modes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of the geometry controlled by PVA thickness, energy level diagrams for up-conversion, and PL/FLIM maps comparing emission characteristics across different spacer thicknesses (S00, S20, S65).
paper_structure: The paper establishes a systematic platform using polymer spacers to control emitter-metal separation. It then presents evidence of three distinct regimes—quenching at short range, enhancement via plasmons at intermediate range, and decoupling at large distances—using intensity mapping and lifetime measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides an excellent experimental realization of open quantum system dynamics in nanophotonics, allowing direct measurement of energy relaxation pathways (radiative vs. nonradiative) as a function of engineered coupling strength to plasmonic modes.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Schematic illustration of controlled spatial geometry of up-conversion NCs and silver NWs. Increasing the thickness of the PVA film in the sequence (a)-(c) provides a means to systematically vary their spatial separation.

Fig. 2. (a) SEM image of silver nanowires deposited on a conductive carbon foil. (b) Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) images of nanowires (upper panel) illustrating the surrounding PVP polymer layer, with corresponding images acquired using a through-lens detector (TLD) shown in the lower panel for comparison. (c) Absorbance spectrum of the silver nanowire colloid.

Fig. 3. (a) TEM image of the NaYF4:Er3+/Yb3+ NCs together with a histogram illustrating the statistical size distribution. (b) SEM image of individual NCs dispersed on a glass substrate (S00) and the corresponding PL image of the same sample area (c). Only minimal agglomeration is observed, which is easily distinguishable in both SEM and PL images. (d) Emission spectrum of a single NC under 980 nm excitation.

Fig. 4. Photoluminescence intensity maps of individual up-conversion NCs acquired for samples S00, S20, and S65 (a-c), together with the corresponding maps of elastically back-scattered laser light (d-f), illustrating the spatial distribution of NWs. The white dashed lines indicate the positions of the NWs. The PL maps were obtained by recording the red up- conversion emission of the NCs under 980 nm laser excitation. The inset in panel (a) shows an SEM image of a bare silver nanowire with attached nanocrystals. The scale bar represents 200 nm.

Fig. 5. μs-FLIM maps of the up-conversion emission recorded for sample S20, acquired from the same sample region as shown in Fig. 4b,e. Panel (a) shows the green emission, while panel (b) corresponds to the red emission of the NCs. Both maps were obtained under 980 nm laser excitation using a pulsed excitation scheme with a pulse duration of 20 µs. The color scale represents the extracted luminescence lifetime values.
